title: Plan back from the goal
caption: Backward reasoning starts from the goal and breaks it into what must be true before it, until it reaches where you stand today.
board: The goal broken down, read from right to left

goal.text: 20 June: everyone celebrates together and gets home safely

shuttle.text: Shuttle back after the open bar

rules.outcome: State the goal as an outcome. It tells you when you are done.
rules.external: Mark what is outside your control. Plan around it.
rules.orphan: Look for tasks the draft left unowned. In this example, they appear under a subgoal.

pappus-and-polya.description: analysis starts from what is required, takes it for granted, and asks from what antecedent it could be derived, until it reaches something already known; Pólya’s entry calls it “working backwards” [1].

polya-how-to-solve-it.title: Pólya, How to Solve It (1945), entries Pappus and Working backwards

regression-in-planning.description: in AI planning, each backward step adds the action’s preconditions to the goal, and each precondition is a dependency the plan needs [1].

russell-norvig-planning.title: Russell and Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, 2nd ed., chapter 11 Planning

fewer-actions-to-consider.description: backward search considers only relevant actions; in the textbook air cargo problem about 1000 actions lead forward and 20 work backward, for that one problem only [1].

russell-norvig-planning.title: Russell and Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, 2nd ed., chapter 11 Planning

it-feels-wrong.description: Pólya notes a psychological difficulty in turning around and not following the direct path to the end [1].

polya-how-to-solve-it.title: Pólya, How to Solve It (1945), entries Pappus and Working backwards

project-management-does-it-too.description: in the Critical Path Method, Kelley and Walker compute the latest time each event may occur “relative to a fixed project completion time”; neither this paper nor the NASA handbook uses the phrase “backward pass”, which is later textbook vocabulary [1].

kelley-walker-critical-path.title: Kelley and Walker, Critical-Path Planning and Scheduling (Proceedings of the Eastern Joint Computer Conference, 1959)

what-the-backward-run-gives.description: a job whose maximum available time equals its duration is critical, because a delay in it delays the project; the method takes the jobs and dependencies as given and is not shown to find missing tasks, so that use here is an inference [1].

kelley-walker-critical-path.title: Kelley and Walker, Critical-Path Planning and Scheduling (Proceedings of the Eastern Joint Computer Conference, 1959)

scope-starts-at-the-end-product.header: Scope starts at the end product
scope-starts-at-the-end-product.description: the NASA handbook says a work breakdown structure begins with the end item and successively subdivides it, and calls it “a product-oriented structure, not an organizational structure” [1].

nasa-wbs-handbook.title: Sadler, NASA Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) Handbook (NASA/SP-20250006071)

vendors-say-clear-goals.description: Anthropic names the best-fit tasks for agents as those with clear success criteria and feedback loops, such as code that automated tests can verify; this is guidance, not a measurement [1].

missing-detail-costs-accuracy.description: models infer unstated requirements 41.1% of the time, prompts that omit requirements are twice as likely to regress when the model or prompt changes, and accuracy sometimes drops by more than 20% [1].

yang-what-prompts-dont-say.title: Yang et al., What Prompts Don’t Say: Understanding and Managing Underspecification in LLM Prompts

asking-recovers-it-and-the-limit.header: Asking recovers it, and the limit
asking-recovers-it-and-the-limit.description: on an underspecified coding benchmark, interacting to ask questions gained up to 74% over not asking, a ceiling and not an average; no source isolates a clear goal as a single variable, so the claim is that missing detail hurts and recovering it helps [1].

vijayvargiya-ambig-swe.title: Vijayvargiya et al., Ambig-SWE: Interactive Agents to Overcome Underspecificity in Software Engineering

start-at-the-goal.title: Start at the goal
start-at-the-goal.script: Start with the goal and work backwards. Backward reasoning is a plain-language name for something Pólya calls working backwards and AI planning calls regression. You ask what must be true just before the goal, then what must be true before that, and you repeat until you arrive at where you stand today.

state-the-outcome.title: State the outcome
state-the-outcome.script: Write the goal as an outcome and not as an activity. Not book a venue, but everyone celebrates together and gets home safely, because an outcome tells you when you are done and an activity does not.

outside-your-control.title: Outside your control
outside-your-control.script: Next, sort what the plan depends on into what is inside your control and what is outside it. The venue's kitchen is not yours, you cannot change how it works, so you plan around it and make sure whatever you hand it is unmistakable.

the-tasks-nobody-owned.title: The tasks nobody owned
the-tasks-nobody-owned.script: Now work back from gets home safely. In this example, that points to a gap in the draft: people need a ride home after an open bar, so a shuttle is added. Working back from arrival also suggests telling guests to bring warm clothes for six degrees at night. Those are useful questions to ask of this plan, not a guarantee that backward planning will uncover every missing task.

well-known-and-agents-like-it.title: Well known, and agents like it
well-known-and-agents-like-it.script: Planning back from a goal is a familiar project-planning idea. Agent guidance also recommends clear goals and success criteria, though that is guidance rather than a universal measurement. When you hand an agent a task, have you given it the goal or only the activity?
